title: Testing how AI could help improve case readiness in the Crown Court
authors: Amar Morjaria - Deputy Director Digital Delivery and AI

content.content: We want to use court time as effectively as possible. That means making sure that, where possible, cases are ready to proceed when they come before a judge.
As part of our wider work to tackle delays and improve the way the justice system works, HMCTS and the Ministry of Justice are exploring where artificial intelligence (AI) could help.

We are identifying specific problems where technology could support our people, make processes more efficient and ultimately help us provide a better service for everyone who uses our courts and tribunals.

Our focus is on using AI where it can solve real problems, while making sure appropriate safeguards, human oversight and clear governance are in place. We test new tools carefully, learn from how they work in practice and only consider wider use where there is clear evidence of benefit.
In October 2026, we will take another step in that work by beginning a pilot of an AI Case Readiness Assistant at Inner London Crown Court.
Helping staff identify issues earlier
A lot of work happens before a Crown Court case reaches trial.

For a trial to go ahead as planned, important steps must be completed and key information must be available at the right time. If problems or missing information are only identified shortly before a hearing, this can lead to delays or mean the hearing cannot go ahead.
The AI Case Readiness Assistant is being tested to explore whether technology can help court staff identify and track these issues earlier.

The tool uses AI to review case information and identify actions that may still need to be completed. By highlighting potential issues earlier, this could help staff focus on what needs attention and take action earlier to help get cases ready to proceed.

Court staff will review the information identified by the tool and remain responsible for deciding what action, if any, needs to be taken. The Case Readiness Assistant will not make or recommend judicial decisions and will not determine the outcome of a case or how the law should be applied.

As always, listing remains a judicial function. The judiciary continues to engage closely with the development and use of AI across the justice system through the Criminal Courts Improvement Group (CCIG) AI working group, chaired by Mr Justice Johnson, the Deputy Senior Presiding Judge. This group considers how emerging technologies can support efficiency and fairness while maintaining appropriate human oversight and ethical safeguards.
This builds on the approach we have previously outlined for AI at HMCTS, which puts human oversight at the heart of how we develop and test the technology.
Starting small and learning from the pilot
Introducing new technology into the justice system requires care. That is why we are starting with a pilot at Inner London Crown Court rather than immediately introducing the tool more widely.
Working with court staff, we will use the pilot to understand how the technology performs in a real operational environment.

We want to understand whether it helps staff identify outstanding issues earlier, whether it supports more effective case preparation and whether, in practice, it can contribute to better use of court time.
The pilot will also give us an opportunity to learn directly from the people using the tool and understand where it works well and where it may need to improve.
We will use that evidence to inform what happens next. We will only consider taking the technology further if it demonstrates clear value and can be used safely and responsibly.
Our wider approach to AI
This pilot is one part of our wider work to understand how AI could support the administration of justice.

We’ve previously explained how HMCTS is exploring AI to address specific challenges, including work involving transcription and summarisation, anonymisation, and search and assistant capabilities within case management systems.

Technology alone will not solve the pressures facing the justice system. Used carefully and responsibly, it has the potential to help our people to spend their time more effectively and to support the delivery of a justice system that is faster, simpler and easier to use.

title: What owning land or property near a public highway can mean
authors: Joel Roberts, Practice Adviser, Customer Engagement and Development

content.content: Key points in brief

If your property is next to a public highway, it is not always obvious where the highway ends and your land begins. This can affect what land is included in your title, what you can build or change, and who is responsible for different areas.
In practice, this does not usually present a problem, but there are some things to think about.
What is a public highway?
A public highway is land that the public has a right to use to get from one place to another. This can include:

Sometimes the limits of a public highway are easy to identify, with features such as pavements, hedges, fences or walls marking the edge. In other places, it can be harder to tell whether land forms part of the highway. There is no standard width or length that applies in every case.

Many highways are looked after by the local highway authority and maintained at public expense. In these cases, the authority controls the surface of the highway, some of the ground beneath it, and the airspace needed for ordinary use of the highway under section 263 of the Highways Act 1980.
Why does it matter if my property is next to a public highway?

It matters because the boundary between private land and public highway land may not be exact or obvious. If land is part of a public highway, the local highway authority may have legal duties and powers over the highway which affect the ownership, use and control of the land.
This can affect:
In many cases, this does not cause a problem. But it is important to check with the local highway authority if ownership or responsibility is unclear.
Does the red line on a title plan show the exact boundary?
The red line on an HM Land Registry title plan usually shows the general position of the property boundary.
Known as a general boundary, it does not usually show the exact position of the legal boundary.
Most title plans indicate general boundaries only. If this applies, the title plan will say that it shows the general position of the boundaries, not the exact line.
This means the red line is only an indication of the boundary. It is not proof of the exact legal boundary.

This also means that land may appear to be inside the red line on a title plan but not actually be included in the registered title. The opposite can also happen. Land may appear to be outside the red line but still be included in the registered title.
The general boundaries rule does not define or limit how much land can be affected.
Can land inside the red line still be part of a public highway?
Yes. Land may appear to be inside the red line on a title plan but still form part of the public highway, even where this is not mentioned in the title register.
Public highways are not usually included inside the red line on a title plan - one reason why it can be hard to tell exactly where private land ends and the public highway begins.
What happens if the red line appears to include part of a public highway?
If the red line on a title plan appears to include part of a public highway, that part of the highway will usually be excluded from the registered title.
This will include:
This means a title plan may appear to include land that is still subject to public highway rights or control by the local highway authority.
Can land that looks private still be public highway land?
Yes, land that appears to be private may still form part of a public highway.
This can include land such as:
You should not rely on appearance, a fence line or the red line on a title plan to decide whether land is private or part of a public highway.
If you are unsure, check with the local highway authority as any highway rights or requirements will override your private rights.
How can I check if land is part of a public highway?
If you want to check whether land forms part of a public highway, contact your local highway authority. They keep records of public highways and public rights of way.
GOV.UK also explains what public rights of way are, what to do if there is a problem and how to contact the right authority: Rights of way and accessing land: Use public rights of way - GOV.UK
FindMyStreet can also help. It lists streets in England and Wales and shows where a street is, its official name and which highway authority looks after it.
Council websites may also publish guidance about public rights of way (often shortened to ‘PRoW’), including information about encroachment and adopted roads.
Where can I find more information?
You can read more guidance from HM Land Registry and other public bodies. Some guidance is quite complex and mainly written for solicitors and conveyancers.

title: Learning, growing and feeling valued as a developer

content.content: MHCLG Digital has launched early-career opportunities for 5 Junior Developers and 5 Associate Delivery Managers to join our teams in Manchester.
Mohsina, Developer, shares how support from colleagues has helped her build her skills and grow professionally since joining the department as a junior developer back in 2024.
Joining MHCLG Digital

I was hired by the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) through one of their in-person digital recruitment days in Manchester. I remember feeling very welcomed by the team from the moment I arrived for my interview. That feeling continued when I joined, especially during my onboarding. Everyone was very supportive and made me feel comfortable picking up work from the start.
Learning

As a junior developer, I was curious about everything and wanted to understand even the little things. I was always encouraged to ask questions. As my lead developer says, "there is no such thing as a stupid question".

I’d describe my work environment as a perfect, guilt-free platform to learn from senior developers. You get the space try new approaches, learn new techniques, ask questions and grow at your own pace.

I was able to pair with different developers in the team, so I got to see different ways of working and learned a lot from everyone. Over time, this made me more confident, and before long, I started picking up work more independently and suggesting ideas that could make a difference.
Growing

I feel lucky to have been part of the Delta team since I started working in MHCLG. Delta is the main internal platform the department uses to collect data and make payments, and one of the most critical internal services in the department.

What I enjoy most is that we are continually evolving the platform, building new features to meet user needs, and working with a modern and varied technology stack. Every day brings opportunities to learn something new and contribute to work that has a real impact.

The team mostly works with Java, PostgreSQL, AWS and MarkLogic (NoSQL database). I had never even heard of MarkLogic before joining the department, but over time I've developed the skills and confidence to work with it, contribute code and support the platform. Most recently, I was involved in a major server and database upgrade, which was a valuable learning experience.

The role has also given me exposure to DevOps practices and ways of working, which I find particularly exciting. Being able to work across different areas of the technology stack has helped me broaden my skills and gain a better understanding of how large-scale services are built and maintained.
Most importantly, every single member in the Delta team has helped me grow in some way, and help has always been available whenever I needed it.
Feeling heard

I think MHCLG is a perfect example of an inclusive Civil Service environment. We have people from different ethnicities, cultures and backgrounds, and everyone is welcomed and respected for who they are. I’ve always felt that people are given a chance to speak, and that their opinions genuinely matter. For me, that sense of being heard and included is one of the things I value most about working here.
A great place to build your career as a developer

I honestly can't ask for much more from what I've got from the department. This junior developer role opened a new door for me. It has given me the support and opportunities to learn, contribute and grow – and I’m still learning!
If you’re thinking about building your career in software development, I encourage you to take a look at the current Junior Developer opportunities in Manchester. You can apply until 11 October.
Find out more about how you can build your career with us.

title: Don't spark disaster: changing public behaviour as UK wildfire risk grows

content.content: This year, we have seen largescale wildfires decimate landscapes at home and across Europe.
In the UK, wildfires have affected moorland, woodlands, grasslands, farmland and community green spaces close to homes and infrastructure.
In fact, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has announced that he will soon host a wildfire summit, focused on how we can increase our resilience to wildfire.

As we experience more frequent periods of hot, dry weather, activities that once carried relatively little perceived risk can have far greater consequences. Disposable barbecues, campfires, discarded cigarettes, glass bottles and reflective litter can all increase ignition risk.
As Communications Officer at the North York Moors National Park Authority, I have personally seen how a single ignition can escalate into a major incident.
One spark can have a devastating impact
It’s been a year since a wildfire affected around 20 square kilometres of the North York Moors National Park, becoming one of the largest and most prolonged incidents ever faced in the area.

The Fylingdales Moor wildfire began in late June 2025 and wasn't formally closed until 6 months later. An investigation by North Yorkshire Fire & Rescue Service found the most likely cause of the blaze was cooking activity with a gas burner or campfire in a remote part of Langdale Forest.

Strong winds, dry vegetation and underlying peat allowed the fire to breach an initial firebreak and spread rapidly across grazed moorland, while the presence of historic unexploded ordnance from former military training activity added significant complexity and risk to firefighting operations.
A nearby secondary fire that broke out in August was caused by a cigarette, thought to have been discarded by a bystander who had stopped their vehicle to observe the main incident.
Communication needs to encourage behaviour change

The fire highlighted the importance of clear, timely communication and strong partnership working. We need to think differently about how we talk about wildfire risk in the UK, to encourage people to change their behaviour and reduce that risk.

Communicating fire risk is not new to the National Park Authority. When Met Office data indicates particularly dry ground conditions and the potential for fires to spread rapidly, Extreme Fire Risk warning signs are erected at key locations across the North York Moors. Regional media are alerted through a press release, and the public are reminded how to help prevent fires and what to do if they see smoke or flames.
This approach has been effective, but it has largely been a seasonal response to periods of increased risk - a message delivered when conditions require additional caution.

As wildfire risk becomes a recognised consequence of a changing climate, we need to move beyond simply communicating when the risk is high, towards building a wider understanding that wildfire is a growing reality for the UK, not a distant threat associated with other countries.
Behaviour change is a form of climate adaptation
Working for a National Park Authority, I usually encounter climate adaptation through large-scale interventions such as restoring peatlands or reducing flood risk by improving river catchments.
Yet adaptation also depends on the cumulative effect of everyday decisions. For wildfire, behaviour change is one of the most immediate and cost-effective forms of climate adaptation available to us.

It is important that we avoid the potentially dangerous assumption that wildfires are caused only by deliberate or reckless behaviour, rather than recognising that risk also exists when everyday activities are carried out in hazardous conditions.
The challenge is not simply to tell people what to avoid, but to help them understand that the environmental conditions in which those actions take place have changed.
Don’t Spark Disaster

In 2026, we have taken a different tack. ‘Don’t Spark Disaster’ has been designed as a broader, longer-term awareness campaign, moving beyond seasonal warnings towards a coordinated approach to wildfire prevention.

A key difference has been the scale of partnership involvement, bringing together North Yorkshire’s two National Parks with those working across the Fire and Rescue service, forestry, tourism and the wider Local Resilience Forum. This has enabled wildfire prevention messaging to extend beyond a single National Park boundary and across North Yorkshire.

What has been particularly striking is the level of engagement with the campaign’s educational content. Videos showing the heat generated by disposable barbecues through an infrared camera proved especially effective in helping audiences visualise the risks associated with these items in dry conditions.

Partnerships with online creators such as Whitby Mumbler and Muslim Hikers have also helped us explore lighter, more accessible ways of encouraging lower-risk choices, such as swapping barbecues for picnic foods that require no cooking. This messaging is backed up by increased patrols at higher-risk locations, with Assistant and Voluntary Rangers providing advice and reinforcing the campaign’s fire safety messages.

The early results suggest that practical, relatable wildfire prevention messages can achieve significant public engagement. As the campaign develops, we will continue building on this foundation, exploring how positive messages around responsible countryside enjoyment can support a stronger culture of wildfire prevention. As with any campaign linked to climate and environmental risk, responses have not been universally positive. Some people remain sceptical about the seriousness of climate change or its connection to wildfire risk. Our approach has been to respond with clear evidence, scientific fact and trusted sources of information.

As wildfire becomes recognised as a domestic climate risk, National Parks have an important role in supporting adaptation at a landscape scale, while also helping people understand how these changes affect the places they live, work and enjoy.
Wildfire resilience involves many aspects of landscape management, including work to restore healthy peatlands that retain water and are better able to withstand dry conditions.

But alongside this, one area where communities and visitors can have an immediate impact is reducing avoidable ignitions. By helping people understand how everyday actions interact with changing environmental conditions, we can support a stronger culture of prevention and help protect the landscapes we all value.

description: Nina tells us about the impact of wildfires on the North York Moors, and how her team are adapting their public communications to meet this evolving risk.

title: Forests and people: why managing forests for people matters

content.content: Many of our woodlands and forests have been shaped over the decades as much by people as by soil, water and climate. From supporting health and wellbeing to strengthening local economies and communities, trees and forests remain a vital part of our everyday lives.
The UKFS recognises this and provides woodland owners with a framework to managing people’s use of forests alongside wider management objectives such as biodiversity and timber production.
Why managing forests for people matters

From small community woodlands to larger forests, UK woodlands deliver a wide range of social and economic benefits. They provide places to exercise and relax, spaces for learning, and opportunities for volunteering and employment. Demand for access to green space is growing, but Natural England research shows access inequalities persist across different communities.1
Woodlands can help address both demand and inequality, which is why the UKFS encourages forest management that:

For woodland managers, this isn’t about opening every site to all activities. It’s about making evidence-based decisions that reflect a woodland’s sensitivities, objectives and local context. In return, visitors can help care for the woodland and report problems, such as antisocial behaviour or wildfire, so that they can be dealt with quickly.
Health and wellbeing benefits

Evidence of the positive impacts of trees and woodlands on physical and mental health continues to grow. Regular access to green spaces is linked to improved mental wellbeing and reduced stress levels.2
The UKFS supports woodland managers by encouraging:

Where managers experience issues such as informal path creation or anti‑social behaviour, positive access management can help guide people to suitable areas while reducing pressure on sensitive habitats.
Forests for everyone

Public access is one of the most visible aspects of people’s connection to forests. The UKFS supports appropriate and well‑managed access, highlighting legal responsibilities and providing a set of key principles including:
Where managers face issues such as conflict between users or pressure on infrastructure, the UKFS provides a clear rationale for zoning, seasonal restrictions or managed routes.
In addition, not everyone experiences forests in the same way and barriers to access can include physical ability, confidence, cultural perception and location.

The UKFS highlights legal requirements for equality and encourages inclusive design and engagement with underrepresented groups, for example people with reduced mobility, to make sure that everyone’s needs are met wherever possible. One of the key principles is the need to remove unintentional barriers and avoid introducing new ones, such as removing stiles where they aren’t needed or replacing steps with a ramp. Addressing this helps to ensure forests benefit everyone, not just those already confident in visiting them.
Supporting the rural economy

Woodlands are central to local and rural economies, creating and supporting jobs in forestry, recreation, tourism, education and land management. Recent Forestry Commission experimental research suggests that the contribution of forest recreation and leisure businesses to the UK economy is significant.3

The UKFS highlights how recreation and tourism can sit well alongside timber and conservation objectives. Well-managed access can support local businesses, such as accommodation and hospitality providers by offering high quality places to visit. Commercial recreation activities such as high rope courses and children’s play trails can also contribute in a sustainable way.
For woodland managers navigating multiple management objectives, the UKFS supports transparent decision making and collaboration with local partners.
Forests are powerful learning environments

Forests and woodlands can also offer learning opportunities from early years exploration to vocational training. The UKFS encourages collaboration with learning providers, helping to deepen people’s connection with the natural world and to build forestry skills for the future.

Educational use needn’t be large scale. Simple interpretation boards can support self‑led learning and occasional visits can be accommodated in many woodlands with good planning. Partnerships help manage expectations and responsibilities as well as building stronger relationships with the local community.

Well‑managed educational access can also improve the public’s understanding of forestry practices. This can help to address concerns about harvesting or forestry operations, and strengthen public support for woodlands and the timber and forestry industries.
Working with local communities
Engaging communities can transform how woodlands are valued and cared for. The UKFS promotes positive community involvement, from volunteering and citizen science to participatory planning.

By involving people early and clearly explaining decisions, managers can build trust and shared responsibility, while retaining professional oversight of management and forestry operations. They can also tap into valuable local knowledge.

Putting the UKFS into practice

For woodland managers, the UKFS offers a practical framework for responding to real world challenges. It helps manage public benefits alongside sustainable management, aiding decisions that are evidence-based, transparent and support the long-term health of people and forests.
By planning for people as carefully as we plan for trees, we can ensure forests remain places that support health, learning, livelihoods and community wellbeing – now and for generations to come.

title: Assembling architects to improve local public services

content.content: Government Digital Service (GDS) recently brought together dozens of architects from across local government and central government for the first Architects Assemble event, hosted by the Local Government Association in London. While attendees came from different organisations and disciplines, they shared a common goal: improving local public services through better collaboration, better decision making, and firmer foundations for technology, digital and data. Architecture often happens behind the scenes, helping organisations navigate complexity, make informed decisions and deliver change. Yet many of the challenges we face are shared across the sector.  Architects Assemble was designed to create space for people to connect and learn from one another, through three workshops and general discussion, to explore how we can start to tackle those challenges together.
Growing adoption of the Local Government Architecture Model
The first workshop explored how wider adoption of the Local Government Architecture Model (LGAM) could be achieved across the sector.
Participants discussed what would give councils the confidence to adopt the model and the factors that are most important when deciding whether to invest time and effort in a new approach.

The discussion then focused on practical application, exploring what would make the LGAM easier to use in day-to-day architecture and transformation work. There was a strong emphasis on ensuring the model is accessible, actionable and relevant to the challenges councils face.
Finally, participants considered what GDS could do over the next 12 months to make the LGAM feel indispensable to everyday practice.
The discussion generated a wealth of ideas that will help shape the next phase of the model's development by GDS Local and designs for the adoption approach.
Creating the conditions for better decisions
The second workshop focused on how better architectural decision making can help create firmer foundations for local government technology, digital and data.

Participants explored how better decision making can help organisations move beyond short-term choices and create the conditions for long-term success. This included discussions about governance, standards, strategic planning and how architecture can provide a framework for making consistent decisions across organisations.

A recurring theme was that stronger foundations are not created through technology alone. They require clear outcomes, shared understanding and better alignment between business, data, digital and technology perspectives.
Building a public sector architecture community
The third workshop focused on building and sustaining a thriving community of practice for architects working to improve local public services.

Many participants recognised that they are often tackling similar challenges, whether related to service transformation, data sharing, organisational change or technology modernisation. Creating opportunities to connect enables people to learn from one another, share what works and avoid solving the same problems repeatedly.

The discussions generated a range of ideas for how the community can continue to develop, including opportunities for peer support, sharing patterns and practices, showcasing work from across the sector and creating more regular opportunities for collaboration.  The aim is to put in place a monthly community webinar, hold quarterly face to face workshops, and extend the community to people who don't have "architect" in their job title.
Looking ahead
Architects Assemble was never intended to be a one-off event.
The conversations throughout the day demonstrated both the value of bringing architects together and the appetite for continued collaboration.

Whether discussing adoption of the LGAM, creating firmer foundations for technology, digital and data, or growing a sustainable community of practice, participants were united by a common ambition: improving public services on a local and national scale.
The challenges facing the sector are significant, but so is the collective expertise, experience and willingness to collaborate.

By continuing to connect architects from across organisations and disciplines, we can help create the conditions for better decisions, firmer foundations and ultimately better outcomes for communities.
If you’re interested in following or getting involved in GDS’s work in this space, sign up to the GDS Local Newsletter.

title: Get Tech Certified 2026: build your technology and digital skills for free
authors: Angie Jones, Communications and Engagement Lead, Government Digital Service

content.content: Today, Get Tech Certified 2026 opens to people working across the UK public sector, offering free digital and technology learning pathways and recognised certifications.

Whether you’re exploring technology for the first time, looking to build your confidence or already working in a digital and technology role and want to deepen your expertise, there’s a pathway for you.
Get Tech Certified runs from 1 October to 31 December 2026, giving you three months to explore the learning available and build skills that can support you in your current role and beyond.
Free learning from leading technology providers

Get Tech Certified is delivered by Government Digital and Data in partnership with leading technology providers, bringing high-quality industry learning and certification opportunities to people working across the UK public sector – for free.
Get Tech Certified is available to eligible civil and public servants. Contractors are not eligible to take part in the campaign.

Our participating providers include some of the organisations developing and delivering the technologies used across industry and the public sector, including Amazon Web Services (AWS), Celonis, Databricks, Datadog, Google, HashiCorp, Microsoft, MongoDB, Oracle, ProsperOps, Science and Technology Facilities Council UKRI, ServiceNow, Snowflake and WSO2.

Through Get Tech Certified, participating providers are making a wide range of digital and technology learning opportunities and recognised certifications available at no cost. This gives you the opportunity to develop practical, relevant skills through learning created by organisations with deep expertise in their technologies and subject areas.

There are opportunities for different levels of experience too. Whether you’re taking your first steps into a subject, developing skills you already use in your role or looking for more advanced learning and certification, you can choose a pathway that works for you.
This year, you can explore learning across:
Building digital and technology capability across the public sector
Technology continues to change how government and public services work.

Building digital and technology capability across the public sector is not only about developing specialist technologists. It is also about giving people across different professions and organisations the skills and confidence to understand and make the most of technology in their work.
Get Tech Certified helps make these development opportunities more accessible by bringing together free learning from leading technology providers in one place.

For individuals, that could mean developing skills that help you in your current role, exploring a completely new area of technology or gaining a recognised certification that supports your professional development.
For teams and organisations, it is an opportunity to encourage continuous learning and strengthen digital and technology capability across the workforce.
Building on Get Tech Certified 2025
Last year demonstrated the appetite for digital and technology learning across the public sector.

In 2025, Get Tech Certified attracted more than 10,000 sign-ups across 336 public sector organisations, giving colleagues access to thousands of free learning opportunities across a range of digital and technology skills.
Learners achieved more than 1,200 recognised certifications through the campaign, helping colleagues build and demonstrate their digital and technology skills.
In 2026, we want to build on that momentum and encourage even more people from across the public sector to take advantage of the learning available.
Whether you work in central or local government, health, education or another public sector organisation, Get Tech Certified provides an opportunity to invest in your digital and technology skills.
Supporting Women in Tech
This year, Get Tech Certified also includes a dedicated Women in Tech strand, supporting more women to explore opportunities, develop their skills and progress in digital and technology.

Throughout the campaign, we’ll be highlighting learning opportunities, case studies, communities and events designed to encourage and support women at different stages of their digital and technology careers. Look out for a Women in Tech blog post coming soon and find out more about what's is available as part of this strand on our hub page.
Find the pathway for you
Getting started is simple.

Visit the Government Digital and Data Hub to explore the learning available from participating technology providers. You can find out what each pathway offers, consider which opportunities best match your interests, experience and development goals, and follow the information provided to start learning.
You don’t need to be a technology expert to Get Tech Certified.

Whether you want to learn something new, build on your existing expertise, gain a recognised certification or explore where digital and technology skills could take you next, there’s an opportunity to get involved.

Get Tech Certified 2026 runs until 31 December 2026. Any free certification vouchers available through the campaign must be claimed by 31 December 2026. Once claimed, you may have additional time to use your voucher, often up to six months, so you do not necessarily need to complete your certification by 31 December. Redemption periods vary by provider, so please check the relevant learning page for the specific redemption period and any provider-specific deadlines.
Explore the learning pathways and start building your digital and technology skills for free.

title: Helping probation practitioners spend less time searching and more time supporting people

content.content: When probation practitioners take on a new case, they often need to quickly understand a person's history, risks and support needs. That information is stored in Delius, the main case management system used across probation, where more than 40 million contact logs are recorded each year.

Finding the right information among thousands of records isn't always straightforward. Different practitioners may use different terminology, acronyms, abbreviations or spellings to describe the same thing, making it difficult to know exactly what to search for.

To address this challenge, colleagues from the Delius team, Probation Data Science and Technical Architecture worked together to improve how search works within Delius, helping practitioners find relevant information more quickly and with less effort.
Why existing search wasn't always enough

In October 2021, Delius introduced a free text search function that allowed practitioners to search contact logs using specific words, phrases and acronyms. While useful, feedback showed that finding information often depended on knowing the exact terms used by the person who originally recorded the contact.

For example, one practitioner might record information about "smoking" while another writes "cigarettes". Someone searching could try several related terms before feeling confident they had found everything relevant. The team saw this pattern repeatedly in service data, with users carrying out multiple searches using similar words to avoid missing important information.
For practitioners managing risk, preparing for appointments or taking over cases from colleagues, that extra effort can add up.

Practitioners can be assigned new cases from colleagues due to resourcing, risk, and expertise. So, they are reviewing their own contacts, but sometimes contacts written by colleagues too. Over time, feedback from users showed clear pain points with the search:

These pain points were most clearly evidenced as “search flurries” - users typing different related terms to double check nothing had been missed in their search e.g. smoking, cigarettes.  Our teams were determined to improve this, so we brought together technical colleagues including Probation Data Scientists and Technical Architects to work collaboratively and investigate areas for improvement.
After analysing the Free Text Search audit log, our team estimated these flurries, and search gaps more generally and found it was using up a meaningful amount of staff time.

Probation Data Science then completed an evaluation of search models and ran a thorough ethical evaluation. The model recommendation was then passed on to the Probation Integration Team who deployed the updated search in October 2025.
Building a better search experience

The team explored different approaches and carried out detailed evaluation work to understand what would best meet users' needs. They ultimately introduced a new hybrid search experience that combines traditional keyword search with technology capable of recognising related meanings, common misspellings and probation-specific terminology.

You can read more data science details about this project on MoJ: nDelius Contact Log Semantic Search - GOV.UK.
Establishing trust from the start
Responsible use of data and technology was a core part of the project

Ethical considerations were built in from the start and reviewed throughout.We designed our product in line with the Ministry of Justice AI and Data Science Ethics Framework that was produced in collaboration with the Alan Turing Institute.

We did a range of analyses to quantify the real impact of any potential bias on the model outputs. We investigated group associations (e.g. male / female) with concepts (e.g. violence / pacifism). We used both theoretical analysis (WEAT testing) and product-specific testing on 30,000 probation contacts, finding no overall evidence of systematic bias.
We do ongoing monitoring and get additional feedback from users to mitigate any bias risk and improve the product.
Putting the new search into practice
After deployment, we did some initial monitoring for feedback from our users (probation practitioners) and the in-built thumbs up / down but those provided little context.

Quantitative analysis revealed how difficult it can be to track time savings, due to difficulties defining and interpreting user behaviour (search flurries). The proportion of time lost on flurries and average time between consecutive searches saw small changes, although usage of Free Text Search has significantly increased over the last half year.

Instead, we relied on User Research to evaluate whether the semantic search model reduced search effort and cognitive load, whilst maintaining trust and confidence in the search results. We were able to validate reduced effort and load in most user cases, with trust remaining high. Although effort was not entirely removed, with it shifting to choosing the right terms and judging results, especially for broad terms.
The impact was most evident when practitioners began using the improved search in real-life situations.
One Performance Quality Officer told the team: "I think it is amazing. It cut down that need to have to read everything."
A Referral Hub Officer described the search as: "Pretty much instant, if the information is there."
And a Senior Probation Officer working in Electronic Monitoring said: "Very easy to use. Our team would be lost without it."
Three Reflections
As with any service improvement, the launch provided valuable insights that will help shape future development.
The work doesn’t stop here
We jointly worked with the Delius team to prioritise next steps.

Firstly, we are working with the Delius team to do a small-scale communications plan for promoting the free text search and particularly help and guidance as that was a shortcoming observed during user research; we will work with Regional IT trainers and Change Management teams to offer a suite of online resources and potentially in-person training.

Secondly, we will work with Technical Architects to rollout the semantic search to a new probation digital service which launched nationally in April 2026 to help practitioners manage their caseload (Manage a Person on Probation, also called MPOP).
We will continue to monitor usage, learn from feedback and look for new opportunities to improve the service.

This project has shown how small improvements to everyday tools can make a real difference. When probation practitioners can find the right information more quickly and with less effort, they can spend more time focusing on what matters most: supporting people, managing risk and protecting the public.

title: Understanding surrogate outcomes in cancer screening research trials

content.content: Health system leaders and policymakers attended a Cancer Research UK (CRUK) event to get an insight into the UK National Screening Committee (UK NSC) position on the use of surrogate outcomes in cancer screening trials.
The CRUK Early Diagnosis Event Series session raised awareness of the UK National Screening Committee’s (UK NSC) newly published position statement on surrogate outcomes in cancer screening trials.

The event was chaired by UK NSC Chair Prof Sir Mike Richards and speakers included Prof Anne Mackie (UK NSC Director of Screening), Dr Sarah Batson (Assistant Professor at University of Warwick), Dr Tasmin Sommerfield (Scottish Director of Screening), and Dr Lisa Douet (National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) Scientific Advisor).
Read the CRUK summary report of the event: Understanding surrogate outcomes in cancer screening trials: implications for screening policy and practice.
Why alternative indicators of screening effectiveness would be helpful
The UK NSC only recommends a screening programme if evidence shows that its benefits would outweigh any harms.

The gold-standard measure of effectiveness for any cancer screening programme is achieving a reduction in deaths from that cancer. However, it can take many years or even decades to collect the cancer-specific mortality data required from large trials.

Academics have therefore been looking for alternative measurements or indicators of screening effectiveness. These outcomes act as a ‘surrogate’ for the desired outcome of mortality reduction before that long-term data is available.
To date, the most promising surrogate outcomes proposed for cancer screening trials have included:
However, the evidence is not yet strong enough for surrogate outcomes to replace cancer mortality as the definitive measure of the overall benefit of screening.

This is because finding more cancers at an earlier stage does not necessarily mean fewer people will die from cancer. Additional cancers detected may be very slow-growing or may never cause harm during a person's lifetime. In addition, what is considered a ‘late-stage’ cancer varies between cancer types, and the link between surrogate outcomes and cancer mortality is not the same for all cancers.
Implications and next steps
The CRUK event provided an overview of the UK NSC’s position statement on surrogate outcomes and explored its implications for health system leaders and policymakers.

Overall, the session reinforced the committee’s view that surrogate outcomes can inform screening research, evaluation and policy discussions, but cannot yet replace cancer-specific mortality as the main measure of cancer screening benefit.
Attendees heard that while a reduction in late-stage disease is encouraging as a surrogate outcome, it is not yet sufficient to demonstrate the benefit of screening.

Participants explored how health systems can try to make evidence-informed decisions in the face of uncertainty. They also discussed the use of in-service evaluations (ISEs) as an important approach to generating evidence in real-world settings.
The summary report concludes with actions and next steps for policy makers and researchers to consider when shaping the future of cancer screening.

title: How does the Environment Agency manage abstraction to protect the environment?

content.content: Water is essential for drinking, farming, industry, wildlife and recreation. Sustainable water abstraction is essential to ensure that river flows and groundwater levels support ecology and natural resilience. We work side by side with abstractors, combining their knowledge of the land with ours, to safeguard the environment and balance the needs of the society, the economy, industry and farmers over the long term.

The pressures are real: floods and droughts are hitting harder and more often. 2026 has seen the driest July in 190 years, with just 5 per cent of expected rainfall and the joint hottest August on record.  The summer overall saw 64 per cent of expected rainfall, resulting in a very difficult harvest for farmers and impacts on fish stocks, bird populations, and wider ecosystems. New research has shown we need 120 per cent of typical rainfall over the next seven months for all areas to be considered out of drought.

This has placed significant demands on abstraction, particularly for irrigation, and agricultural reservoir stocks have declined rapidly, especially where abstractors rely heavily on storage. If you own, operate or are planning to build a reservoir, our new planning guides explain the requirements.
What are abstraction licences?

Abstraction is the process of taking water from a river, lake or groundwater source for uses such as irrigation, industry, recreation or drinking water. We grant abstraction licences to protect the environment and the rights of existing lawful water users.
Those with abstraction licences are allowed to take water in line with the conditions of their licence.

Abstracting more than 20 cubic metres a day generally requires a licence, though some activities, such as firefighting, are exempt. If you take water from the same source at multiple points, the combined total must be 20 cubic metres or less a day to qualify for exemption.

If you don't hold a licence, you may be able to agree a trade or share with an existing licence holder, permanently or temporarily, provided all licence conditions can still be met. Where an abstraction is moved to a different abstraction point, the buyer of the abstraction right would normally have to apply for their own licence or change their existing licence if they have one.
Not all activities require an abstraction licence to take place with some being exempt.
Abstraction licence holders can manage their accounts online to see a summary of their licence and past returns.
How can the Environment Agency restrict abstraction?
There are two main types of restrictions that the Environment Agency can implement on abstractors at times of pressure: hands-off flow conditions and Section 57 restrictions.

Hands-off flow conditions on licences reduce or prevent abstraction to protect other abstractors and the environment. Many of these restrictions have come into effect in 2026 due to very low river flows. Licence holders who have hands-off flow condition on their licences will be notified when the condition comes into force, with as much advance notice as possible.
Section 57 of the Water Resources Act 1991 allows formal notices to be issued to holders of spray irrigation abstraction licences to protect river flows during drought throughout a catchment.
Spray irrigation abstraction licence holders can help make the most of the water which their licence authorises to take by:
Environment Agency updated prospects for irrigation report for summer 2026 can be found on gov.uk.

We work closely with farmers, the National Farmers Union (NFU), Water Abstraction Groups (WAGs) and Internal Drainage Boards (IDBs) to give as much advanced notice as possible before stopping or reducing conditions are needed on abstraction licences to protect the environment.
We continue to carry out irrigation patrols and other compliance checks to ensure all abstractors are complying with their licence conditions to help protect water availability.

If abstractors believe that they may not be able to comply with their abstraction licence or have issues accessing water supplies, they should contact their local area Environment Agency office for further advice as soon as possible.
What support is available for those with abstraction licences who may have restrictions in place?

Drought is putting real pressure on farmers this year. From Thursday 1 October, we're letting abstraction licence holders start refilling their water storage reservoirs early, typically a month ahead of schedule. This temporary Regulatory Position Statement runs from 1 October to 31 October.
Eligible licence holders can act now, without waiting for a local Environment Agency drought assessment. At a time when every week counts, this means farmers can secure water when they need it most.

This isn't a blanket relaxation of the rules. Protecting wildlife and sensitive water environments means some tough decisions: the RPS does not apply to Principal Salmon Rivers or to catchments with a section 57 spray irrigation restriction in place. Where drought restrictions already apply, abstraction stays restricted. Existing licence conditions, including hands-off flow and level constraints, remain in force.
Wider general guidance is available for abstraction licence holders affected by prolonged dry weather and drought, alongside short and long-term options to improve water access and resilience.
We also have policy positions that allow farmers to take water during flood conditions, supporting opportunities to capture high flows whilst continuing to protect rivers and the wider environment.
For short term support:
Managing abstraction for the long term

We know that getting a long duration abstraction licence has been difficult, and that this has held back investment in sustainable abstraction, including farm storage reservoirs. We have therefore changed how we assess long duration abstraction licence requests, and the evidence needed to support them, for those who don't currently hold a licence. This should make it easier to invest for the long term. New applicants can find out more here.

For existing abstractors, there are a number of schemes that can help generate water resilience. For more information on these schemes and how to manage your land and farm in dry weather, including information on looking after livestock, managing farm reservoirs, storing flammable materials and creating firebreaks please visit the Defra Farming Blog.

We’re encouraging the establishment of Water Abstractor Groups (WAGs) to work together to understand and jointly plan for their future water needs. Defra provided funding to Regional Water Resources Groups to support these activities and updated guidance to help farmers setup Water Abstractor Groups.

We also recently launched the latest round of Local Resource Option (LRO) Screening Studies, helping groups of farmers identify practical solutions for long-term water resilience. The 2026/27 application window is now closed and projects selected, but further projects may be offered on a first-come-first-served basis if funds remain. Contact WRAgriculture@environment-agency.gov.uk for details.
Reporting incidents
If you are out and about, please report incidents to our hotline - 0800 80 70 60.
It's free and open 24 hours a day.
Incidents you should report include:
More information on other incidents and how to report can be found on gov.uk.
For any further questions you can call our National Customer Contact Centre on 03708 506 506.

title: Help for first time directors: Training and resources from the Institute of Directors (IoD)
authors: Hugo Legh - Head of External Affairs, Institute of Directors

content.content: The Institute of Directors (IoD) supports directors and senior leaders in their careers. It provides practical guidance, professional development opportunities and resources to help you lead with confidence and impact.
Becoming a director is a significant career step, but it also brings new responsibilities. The IoD Boardroom Foundations and Code of Conduct resources can:
Understanding your role as a director

As a new director, you'll likely already have extensive senior experience. But taking on board-level responsibility is a different proposition from managing the day-to-day. You’ll need to understand your legal duties and governance obligations, balance the interests of your stakeholders and keep the long-term success of your organisation firmly in view.
Understanding this early will help you navigate complex decisions, ask the right questions and make an impact in the boardroom.
Build confidence with Boardroom Essentials
If you’re new to the boardroom – or are hoping to be appointed in the future – the IoD’s free Boardroom Essentials course gives you a solid grounding in what a director role realistically involves.
You’ll get practical guidance on the areas you’ll need to understand, including:
A framework for responsible leadership

Knowing your responsibilities matters. But it's just as important to understand the standards you're expected to uphold. That’s where the IoD Code of Conduct for Directors comes in. It’s a practical framework for ethical, responsible leadership, setting out the principles you’ll need to demonstrate integrity, accountability and professionalism in the boardroom.
It’s a resource you’ll return to throughout your directorship, particularly when you’re weighing up your responsibilities or working through a difficult situation.
The benefits of continued professional development

Investing in your professional development brings benefits beyond growth on an individual level. As your knowledge, judgement and confidence develops, you’ll be better equipped to contribute effectively in the boardroom. It can support your organisation in strengthening its performance, make better decisions and create sustainable value.
That’s the Director Dividend: the personal and organisational return generated by more capable, informed and effective directors.

title: My first day at Natural England: sustainable development for people and nature

content.content: Reflections from Neil Hornby, Chief Executive of Natural England

In this blog, Neil Hornby marks their first day as Chief Executive of Natural England with a visit to Kent to see how housing development and nature recovery can work hand in hand. Reflecting on a new Operational Statement that lets Natural England focus its planning advice where it matters most, and on early progress through the Nature Restoration Fund and the Norfolk Environmental Delivery Plan, Neil sets out a vision for an organisation that is ambitious for nature, pragmatic in its approach, and genuinely collaborative with developers, farmers and communities alike.

I wanted my first day as Chief Executive of Natural England to begin not behind a desk, but out on the ground with colleagues and partners. So today I will visit Kent to meet with Barratt Redrow and see their Conningbrook development – where I will see first-hand how homes, infrastructure and nature recovery can be planned and delivered together. I will also visit a partner’s environmental works, to look at how mitigation for nutrient pollution can be developed.

As Chief Executive, I want Natural England to be ambitious in its efforts to recover nature and be straightforward in the way it works: an organisation that protects and restores nature, uses the best available science and evidence, listens to its customers and partners and delivers effectively. I don’t want us to just be known for identifying environmental risks and issues, but for helping people find solutions that are a win-win for nature and people.

I know I am stepping into a critically important role at a vital time. As we face the twin crises of biodiversity loss and climate change - in one of the most nature-depleted countries in the world - our work to recover nature and improve access to it has never been more important or more urgent.

Too much of the wildlife that inspired my love of nature as a child has been lost and too many people have become disconnected from the natural world. And that’s why I am committed to this important task.

At Conningbrook, I will see a growing community alongside a 3.2 hectare nutrient mitigation wetland. The site is a practical example of development working with nature: early engagement from both the developer and our teams, a clear understanding of environmental pressures and partnership working have helped create space for new homes, green space and addressed impacts on the internationally important Stodmarsh wetland site.
A clear purpose and a focused way of working

That is the approach I want us to build on. Today, Natural England are also publishing a new Operational Statement allowing us to prioritise our planning advice more strategically to have the greatest impact for nature and people. This follows recent changes in the Planning and Infrastructure Act 2025.

Previously, Natural England was required to provide advice on every request relating to development under the Town and Country Planning Act. This meant specialist expertise was spread across a high volume of consultations, including routine cases where established guidance already existed. The amended duty brings our role more closely in line with other statutory consultees.

In practice, this means engaging earlier with local authorities in developing plans and strategic solutions, providing clearer standing advice, standard guidance and evidence for routine or lower-risk proposals, and reserving bespoke input for the most complex cases and those presenting the greatest risks or opportunities for nature.  This approach is intended to provide greater certainty and consistency for local planning authorities and developers while ensuring specialist advice is focused where it can add the greatest value for nature and people.

Statutory consultation requirements remain unchanged, as do the protections for important habitats, species and designated sites. We will continue to fulfil our legal responsibilities and provide responses where planning and environmental legislation requires it.
The new approach will be carefully introduced through a phased approach with partners.
From site-by-site mitigation to work at scale

This focus on strategic engagement and larger scale solutions is already reflected in our work on the Nature Restoration Fund, where developers can make a levy payment towards a coordinated programme of conservation measures, rather than commissioning fragmented mitigation site by site.

Our first draft Environmental Delivery Plan for Norfolk, published for consultation in the last fortnight, builds on our previous work on providing strategic solutions to tackle the impacts of pollution and support the recovery of protected species.

The first plan is intended to help unlock up to 15,780 homes while raising more than £30 million for large-scale improvements to rivers and wetlands, including the Norfolk Broads. We welcome your feedback on this plan as we seek to roll out this important scheme.
My vision for Natural England

Natural England’s core purpose - to achieve nature recovery - is clear and non-negotiable. I’m clear that our strategy, Recovering Nature for Growth, Health and Security, provides the blueprint for the outcomes we seek and how we will achieve them. We must deliver successful nature recovery at scale and across all parts of our country. This will mean developing new approaches and building strong partnerships to ensure that nature’s essential contribution to our economy, health and national security is fully valued.

I want to be relentlessly focused on how Natural England can deliver for nature in a way that is customer focused, collaborative and pragmatic. That means making our advice timely and practical, setting expectations clearly and focusing our expertise where it can achieve the greatest impact. And it means Natural England working in genuine partnership with infrastructure developers, housebuilders, farmers, land managers, businesses, local authorities and communities to deliver shared objectives on growth, clean energy, food security, health and nature recovery together.
Over the coming weeks and months, I look forward to hearing from colleagues, customers and partners about our work together and to exploring opportunities to do more to deliver for people and nature.

title: Rollout begins of in-service evaluation of SMA screening in England

content.content: The in-service evaluation (ISE) of newborn screening for spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is under way in NHS services in England.

From 1 October 2026, babies born in maternity units across the West Midlands are being tested for SMA, a rare but serious genetic condition that affects approximately 1 in 10,000 babies. SMA is being added to the serious conditions that newborn babies are already screened for using the routine newborn blood spot (NBS) screening test.

The UK National Screening Committee (UK NSC) recommended an ISE to assess the feasibility and effectiveness of adding SMA to the NBS screening programme in the long term. ISEs are used to test a change in screening policy if evidence gaps can only be reasonably filled by data collection and evaluation in a live NHS setting. Data from the evaluation will help inform a definitive UK NSC recommendation on whether and how to continue newborn screening for SMA.

After its launch in the Birmingham NBS screening laboratory, the ISE will be rolled out in phases to the 6 other English regional laboratories already participating in the ISE of screening for severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID). The government’s ambition is for the roll-out to then extend to the country’s remaining 6 regional laboratories so that all babies born in England will be offered SMA screening as part of the ISE.

The aim of screening will be to help identify SMA before symptoms develop. When SMA is detected early, babies can be referred promptly for clinical assessment and treatment, which can significantly improve outcomes. Evidence suggests that introducing SMA screening throughout England could, each year, prevent around 3 early deaths, prevent around 2 babies from needing permanent ventilation, prevent around 30 babies from being confined to sitting, and enable around 37 babies to live largely normal lives.
NHS England is updating all its national NBS screening information for professionals and the public to cover the introduction of screening for SMA.

The NBS screening e-learning module on NHSE elfh Hub now includes information about SMA screening. Targeted training sessions are being delivered in advance of the ISE rollout in each screening laboratory to maternity units and staff. Details of these sessions will be shared through existing communication routes.
In addition, SMA UK is launching a campaign, SpotSMA, to raise awareness of the symptoms of the condition among health professionals.
Meanwhile, the Screening tests for you and your baby information is being updated for all parents and there will be a new leaflet for parents of babies who screen positive for SMA.

title: From community meadows to nature corridors: Local Nature Recovery Strategies in action

content.content: Nature recovery needs action at every scale.
We all need to be working together to create the bigger, better and more joined-up network of habitats that nature needs to recover.

From the parish resident planting wildflowers for pollinators, to the farmer creating new habitats on their land. Or the local government planner thinking about how to ensure sustainable development and the water company looking to improve the water quality of a river catchment. We all have a part to play.
That is exactly why Local Nature Recovery Strategies (LNRSs) were created.

Not to sit on a shelf, but to be community-owned plans for environmental improvement that are embedded in the planning system, and that carry weight in public body decision-making. They apply across places and sectors, from neighbourhoods and fields all the way up to counties and catchments.
On 30 September, we announced that Government is supporting local areas to deliver their LNRS through a £26 million investment over the next three years.
This money will support the strategy owners, called ‘responsible authorities’, to keep working with their local partners and communities to better target nature recovery across the country.
In this post, we’ll look at how responsible authorities are already using their LNRSs to help communities and organisations direct efforts where they’ll have the most impact.
Supporting national and local nature priorities, and driving opportunities
LNRSs are developed by responsible authorities in partnership with communities, businesses, land managers, planners and environmental organisations.
They provide a shared blueprint for where action will have the greatest local impact on nature, while contributing to our national environmental priorities.

With most LNRSs now published, we can clearly see the priorities that each community is working on to address their environmental challenges, and the wider national impact their actions will make when combined.

For example, restoring wetlands and floodplains can reduce flood risk for homes and businesses downstream. Creating green corridors and urban tree canopy can cool city streets and protect people's health during heatwaves. Improving soil health and riverside vegetation can filter pollutants and improve water quality in local rivers.
By rooting priorities in local conditions, LNRSs ensure that action for nature delivers tangible benefits for the people who live alongside it, with knock-on benefits that reach much further afield.
Examples of local, grassroots change

In Shropshire, a parish community has been leading efforts to restore meadows in its local area and are already seeing amazing results, demonstrating the difference that can be made when people come together around a shared vision for nature and place. To help build on this momentum, partners across Shropshire have collaborated to create a practical workbook to support town and parish councils in delivering the Shropshire and Telford & Wrekin LNRS in their own communities.

Farmers too are finding LNRSs useful for guiding land management decisions. In Hull and East Yorkshire, the local nature partnership has developed tools to help align Sustainable Farming Incentive and Countryside Stewardship Higher Tier actions with LNRS priorities, making it easier to deliver joined-up outcomes for nature and farm profitability.

Meanwhile across the country, responsible authorities and their partners are exploring ways to support community-led delivery. In the West of England, for example, the new Community Nature Fund is helping communities and local organisations take practical action that contributes to the priorities identified through the region's LNRS.

Whilst in the West Midlands, the new Nature Investment Hub is helping local businesses and investors to connect with impactful projects that might otherwise struggle to get off the ground. Projects on the Hub link directly back to the West Midlands LNRS, showcasing how the project will deliver shared priorities for the area.
Connecting local actions into landscape-scale change
When communities, land managers, businesses, planners and public bodies work from a shared understanding of local priorities, their individual actions can begin to connect.

Small habitat improvements, new wildlife-friendly management practices and local restoration projects can collectively create larger, more resilient networks of nature. LNRSs are designed to support large-scale change like this, by highlighting opportunities where partners could join-up efforts to result in landscape-scale change.
We are already seeing examples of this happening.

The first trees have been planted at Pucklechurch Wood in South Gloucestershire – a 30-hectare site that will form part of the Western Forest, the UK's first new national forest in over three decades.

Stretching from the Cotswolds to the Mendips, the Western Forest aims to plant 20 million trees by 2050, bringing together councils, parish communities, the Forest of Avon and local volunteers in exactly the kind of coordinated, place-based delivery that LNRSs are designed to enable.

LNRSs can also support landscape-scale change in urban areas. In March 2026, a partnership was formed in London to drive forward a new regional park, designed to connect green and blue spaces across west London into a more continuous landscape.

The Mayor of London, responsible authority for London’s LNRS, sits on that partnership. Their LNRS aligns with and supports the new regional park, which will implement one of the green corridors identified in the LNRS.
The regional park will improve biodiversity, climate resilience, access, and long-term economic growth in the area, contributing to many of the priorities and measures set out in the LNRS.
Local leadership for local delivery

The successful development of LNRSs has been a collaborative effort. Responsible authorities have worked closely with local communities, environmental organisations, farmers, businesses, planners and many other partners to create strategies that reflect local priorities. They continue to bring these groups together to turn the proposals set out in LNRSs into action on the ground.
Government’s role now is to help make that local delivery easier, better connected and more impactful.

Through a feedback loop of information from local areas on how delivery is going, we’re able to better understand what is working well, where more support is needed, and where we can make better use of national policy measures to direct investment and action where it can have the most impact.

We’re supporting responsible authorities to provide strategic leadership for environmental delivery and coordinate action in line with their LNRS, and are providing £26 million over the next three years to help them take on this role. Defra bodies, such as the Environment Agency, Forestry Commission and Natural England, are also providing technical expertise, data and delivery support to help translate plans into practical action.
How to play your part in nature’s recovery
Nature recovery clearly depends on collective action.

Every action matters. And when those actions are guided by a shared vision, they have the potential to add up to something much bigger: a healthier, more resilient and more connected natural environment for generations to come.
Are you looking to support nature in your community? Your local LNRS can help identify where your efforts will make the biggest difference.
To find out more about LNRSs or learn how you can contribute to nature recovery in your area, visit GOV.UK or find your local strategy.
